learn.title: Two keys, one slot
learn.body: A collision happens when two different keys hash to the same slot. They cannot be avoided: with more keys than slots, some slot must hold two. Even with fewer keys, collisions come sooner than you expect.

learn.title: Why sooner
learn.body: Think of 23 people in a room. The chance that two share a birthday among 365 days is about one half. Hash tables behave the same way, so any table must have a plan for collisions.

learn.title: Two plans
learn.body: Open addressing keeps everything in the array. On a collision, try the next slot, and the next, until one is free. Separate chaining lets each slot hold a small list of items. The next lessons cover chaining in detail.

learn.title: Linear probing
learn.body: Slots hold -1 when empty. Keys 12, 22 and 7 all hash to slot 2 with size 5, so two of them move on.

learn.title: Placing 22
steps: Try slot 3. It is empty, so 22 goes there
Then 7 % 5 is 2 as well, so it tries 2, 3, then 4

choices: Two keys hashing to the same slot
questions.explanation: Different keys can produce the same index.

questions.prompt: Can collisions be avoided completely when there are more keys than slots?
questions.explanation: With more keys than slots, at least two keys must share a slot.

questions.prompt: With size 5 the keys 12, 22 and 7 all start at which slot?
In linear probing, a key finds its slot taken. What does it do?
questions.explanation: It moves forward one slot at a time, wrapping around at the end.

questions.prompt: Giving each slot its own list of items is called separate \_\_.
questions.explanation: Each slot is the head of a chain of items.

questions.prompt: Match each plan to its idea.
questions.explanation: Both plans deal with collisions in different ways.
